Snowflake is a fully managed cloud SaaS data platform with no self-hosted/on-prem deployment option documented anywhere in the evidence; self-hosting is a category error for this product type, not a missing feature.

Missing for 10: explicit documentation of configuring the retention period (e.g., DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS parameter), explicit purge/permanent-delete commands, and any GDPR/right-to-erasure specific deletion guarantees.

Snowflake documents resource monitors that track credit usage and can auto-suspend a warehouse (or disable an Adaptive Warehouse) when it hits a credit limit, warehouses that auto-suspend/auto-resume and can be started/stopped anytime, per-user quotas (GA), and newer cost-anomaly detection with notification integrations (GA) plus anomaly monitors (preview) — directly matching the 'stop a runaway query or idle compute overnight' story. Community evidence corroborates real-world use of resource monitors as a recommended cost-control practice, though one commenter notes Snowflake lacks query-level cost attribution/recommendations, a real secondary gap. Missing for 10: independent hands-on validation that auto-suspend/resource-monitor limits reliably halt a genuinely runaway single query mid-execution (vs. just capping warehouse-level spend), and more detail on the maturity of the preview anomaly-monitor feature.

Missing for 10: independent/hands-on validation of consistency across multiple consuming tools, and detail on join/versioning governance controls beyond the docs snippets.

Snowflake docs describe Snowpipe as enabling near-real-time loading from staged files, but explicitly frame the latency as 'within minutes' rather than seconds, and the evidence pack contains no mention of the low-latency Snowpipe Streaming API (which targets sub-minute/seconds latency) or its documented client SDK. Streams capture change data but are for CDC consumption, not ingestion. Missing for 10: documentation of Snowpipe Streaming API with seconds-level latency claims, client SDK/API reference for streaming ingestion, and any hands-on/independent confirmation of seconds-level queryability.

Snowflake's Time Travel is well-documented: it allows querying historical data within a defined retention window (data updated/deleted since) and restoring accidentally or intentionally deleted objects such as tables, at individual or container level. This directly matches the story's requirements for both time-based querying and undrop/restore of dropped tables. Missing for 10: no independent/hands-on community corroboration of Time Travel specifically (community evidence covers other topics), and no detail on retention limits across edition tiers.
